articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'The Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments' (Digest No.1)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
abstract: Summary form only given, as follows. The author presents a general overview of the place of user interface systems in the current generation of IPSEs and suggests that the current approach is ad hoc and not based on any systematic analysis of user requirements. As far as has been reported, none of the existing IPSEs have designed their user interfaces from any kind of analysis of software engineering activities. He then discusses what are the key issues and requirements in the design of IPSE user interfaces, in particular the management of complexity, and suggest how appropriate solutions should be discovered. It is particularly important that the developers of IPSE user interfaces export their technology to IPSE users. There are clear technical and organisational difficulties in establishing IPSE UI requirements and these are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
abstract: A user interface is required to match the users perception of the system. Careful design of a system can help by influencing the users perception of the system towards a single common perception for all users. If the system is functionally simple to understand then the task is easier. With a large and complex system such as an IPSE the task is anything but easy. The author looks at how the user interface of one particular IPSE, ISTAR, has developed and how the user is helped by addressing the constraints imposed by these factors is helped.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Generic interface constructs for flexible interaction
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
abstract: The author outlines current work on the human-computer interface to the ASPECT IPSE. A software engineering environment should be distinguished on the one hand from standard operating systems by the high level and integration of the services it provides. On the other hand, it should differ from standard application clusters by the openness it offers to new devices, tools, and users. The first criterion requires genericity, the second flexibility. At the user interface both these requirements have special significance. The ease of design and ease of use of the user interface is critical to the performance and development of the environment as a whole. Ease of design implies that new application interfaces can be developed, or old ones upgraded, with the minimum of cost. Ease of use ensures that productive time is not wasted fighting through to the underlying functionality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
abstract: There is a school of thought which holds that a user is simply one element of a system. This view of the user elements of a system raises the question of why is it therefore necessary to elevate this type of interface into a discipline/skill area in its own right. Cannot conventional system development techniques be used for the specification and implementation of the interfaces to the user elements? The author addresses this question and uses the MMI project within the ECLIPSE programme for illustration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Human factors aspects of the IPSE 2.5 user interface
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of MMI in Software Engineering Environments
abstract: The author discusses the importance of surface features in good MMI design in the context of IPSE 2.5. During the course of the IPSE 2.5 project, which involved the specification and design of user interface components, an IPSE 2.5 house style was explored and represented by a number of standard surface features. Examples of some of these surface features are given with the human factors rationale behind their design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
